1:
The occasion is contested first. Keil and Delitzsch call it an anonymous thanksgiving rather than a supplication, sung with a fresh recollection of a deadly peril, from the lips of an individual who distinguishes himself from the church; they note that the Greek version split it at the tenth verse into two Hallelujah psalms, and that the late date shows in the Aramaic colouring. Adam Clarke takes it for a thanksgiving after the captivity, compared to death and the grave, the return being called the land of the living; he reports that the Syriac supposes it written when Saul came to the mouth of the cave where David lay hidden, and that most of the fathers referred the psalm to the passion and triumph of Christ. John Calvin weighs two candidates: some ascribe it to Hezekiah on his recovery, others to David after the rebellion of Absalom, and the later verse calling all men liars fits a betrayed king better than a convalescent.

The opening clause is disputed too. Charles Ellicott observes that the object has to be supplied, this poet being given to verbs without one, and offers two alternatives: I have longed that the Lord should hear, as the Syriac and Arabic take it, or I am well pleased that he hears, as the Greek and Latin do. Augustine of Hippo presses the received reading. Is it a reason for having loved that the Lord will hear, when we should rather love because he has heard? He answers that hope is wont to inflame love, then asks how the soul knows God has inclined his ear at all, except by saying I have believed — so the three abide, because thou hast believed thou hast hoped, and because thou hast hoped thou hast loved.

C.H. Spurgeon makes the declaration itself the point: it was required under the law but never produced in a human heart except by grace, love being the sweetest of the graces and the surest evidence of salvation. The psalmist knows not only that he loves but why, and when love can justify itself with a reason it is deep and abiding — they say love is blind, but when we love God the affection has its eyes open. Clarke meets the objection that such love is mercenary: no other love can flow from the creature to its Creator, we love him because he first loved us, and love begets love. Calvin hears the abrupt opening as emphatic, a man who could find joy nowhere else, since our hearts wander after fruitless pleasures until God knits them to himself. John Gill grounds the love in the perfections of God’s nature and the works of creation, providence and grace, redemption first. Matthew Henry calls the abruptness fitting, since a profession the heart is full of complies with the first and great commandment, God’s love of compassion requiring our love of complacency in him.

The inclined ear is read as condescension. Henry finds in it both readiness, God laying his ear to the mouth of prayer though it be whispered in groanings that cannot be uttered, and a wonderful stooping. Gill denies that God is hard of hearing and turns the image the same way: he listens when prayers are like the chattering of a crane or a swallow, or only sighs without a voice, and bows his ear as a nurse does to a child. Clarke supplies a situation, a suppliant so sick he could scarcely speak, to whose mouth the Lord bends to catch every word; and he adds that a man who prays much will be emboldened to pray more, since none supplicate the throne of grace in vain. Ellicott finds the second half difficult, the literal text reading and in my days I will call, but there is none; he prefers the common phrase, in the day when I call.
3:
The third verse is worked hard. Adam Clarke renders the first phrase the cables or cords of death and offers two pictures for it: the fetters of a captivity, and the cords by which a criminal is bound for execution. The second phrase he makes the straitnesses of the grave, since there was so little expectation of life that the psalmist speaks as one already condemned, executed and closed up in the tomb. Charles Ellicott prefers to emend: the text gives the oppressions of the grave, but a change in one letter brings the clause closer to the earlier psalm it plainly borrows from, and yields the nets of the grave. He would also keep one verb in both halves, so that the nets catch the psalmist and he in turn catches trouble and sorrow.

Clarke uses the verse against a devotional commonplace. Because the psalm has been used in the thanksgiving of women after a safe delivery, it has been supposed that the pain of childbirth equals for its duration the torments of the damned; this he calls shockingly absurd, since human nature could not endure the wrath of God for a moment, and the body must first die and be rebuilt on indestructible principles before such punishment could be borne. John Gill reads the verse typologically, applying it first to Christ, of whom he takes David a type, a man of sorrows surrounded with sorrow in the garden and dying the accursed death of the cross, and then to David when Saul and his men compassed him about.

Gill takes calling on the name to mean either calling on the Lord for speedy deliverance or calling in the name of the Messiah, the one Mediator. Clarke assigns graciousness to God’s own nature, righteousness to his dealings with men, and mercy to his compassion toward all penitents; Gill notes that this is how the psalmist found him in the act of calling.

Who the simple are draws the most comment. Gill defines them as those of small understanding, whom several old versions call babes: men sensible of their want of wisdom, who commit themselves to the Lord, artless and easily imposed upon by designing men, and therefore preserved from a final falling away, from the snares of the world and the temptations of Satan. Clarke agrees that all the versions render the word little ones and takes it of those meek and lowly of heart who feel the spirit of children; God has a peculiar regard for the young and gives his angels charge concerning them, since otherwise children are exposed to so many dangers that most would fall victims in infancy. Ellicott keeps it lexical: inexperienced, in a good sense, as the word often is in the book of Proverbs.

The address to the soul is read as a homecoming. Clarke makes God the centre toward which all immortal spirits tend and in connection with which alone they find rest, since everything separated from its centre is in a state of violence and, if intelligent, cannot be happy; he allows that the rest may more immediately mean the promised land, and finds in two forms here a mark of the psalm’s late origin. Gill lets the rest mean Christ, a cessation not from doing works but from depending on them, a deliverance from the curse of the law and the tyranny of sin, a peace broken in upon by temptation but returned to as the dove returned to the ark when it could find rest nowhere else. Ellicott adds that this repose is not the worldling’s serenity nor the sensualist’s security, and quite unlike the fool’s address to his soul in the parable, but the repose of a quiet conscience and a trusting heart. Keil and Delitzsch pass over these verses without comment, reserving their note for the profession of faith that follows.
8:
Adam Clarke reads the threefold deliverance as rescue, joy and safe footing: a life snatched from destruction, sorrow turned into joy, and a man taken out of a land of snares and pitfalls into a plain path. He quotes an old Psalter: he took my saule fra dede, my eghen fra teres, my fete fra slippyng. John Gill distributes it across three deaths: a bodily one, when the psalmist was surrounded by an army, in enemy hands at Gath and driven out by his own son; a spiritual one, regeneration being a passing from death to life; and an eternal one, the just wages of sin. Charles Ellicott keeps to the last clause, preferring stumbling to falling and pointing to the older psalm behind it.

The resolution to walk before the Lord is read as a rule of life. C.H. Spurgeon calls it the psalmist’s second resolution, to live as in the sight of God among the sons of men, since a man’s walk is his way of life and some live only as in the sight of their fellows. The truly gracious man considers the presence of God and acts under his all-observing eye, and Spurgeon puts the difference in a sentence: Thou God seest me is a far better influence than My master sees me. Gill grounds the phrase in a comparison, another man’s walking with God being explained by the apostle as pleasing him, and several old versions rendering the clause I will please the Lord; the land of the living he takes for this world or the church, though Jewish commentators find the land of Canaan, a type of where glorified saints dwell for ever. Clarke hears in the verb a deliberate setting out: the eyes brightened so that he can see, the feet strengthened so that he can walk, the soul alive so that he can walk with the living.

Where the psalm ends is itself a question. Clarke reports that five old versions close it here and begin a new one with the profession of faith, a division the Hebrew, Chaldee and Syriac do not acknowledge. Gill calls that groundless, unsupported by the original or the Targum and against the connection with what precedes. Matthew Henry notes the same split without contesting it and passes on the name it acquired, the Martyr’s psalm, from the verse about the death of the saints.

Henry finds three confessions in what follows, of faith, of fear and of gratitude, taking the first as the ground of the speech. What David believed included the assurance given by the prophet that he should exchange his crook for a sceptre; he endured much hardship in that belief, and therefore spoke — to God in prayer and praise, to himself when he told his own soul to return to its rest, and to others, telling his friends what his hope was, though it exasperated the king against him. Those who believe with the heart, he adds, must confess with the mouth, for the glory of God, the encouragement of others, and as evidence of their sincerity. Spurgeon takes the same line from the other end: he could not have spoken so but for his faith, and would never have prayed nor testified had faith not kept him alive; no man should speak about the things of God unless he believes, since the speech of the waverer is mischievous while the tongue of the believer is profitable, and the most powerful speech ever uttered has come from a heart fully persuaded. Gill fills in what the belief contained, not merely that God is but that this God was gracious and his own; and he notes that the apostle applies the words to himself and his fellow ministers. Clarke keeps the struggle in view: the promises were believed throughout, but confidence was hard to maintain, the afflictions being oppressive and of long standing.
11:
John Gill grants that lying is common to man, but denies the charge can be universal, since grace puts it off with the rest of the old man; however degenerate the age, some did not deserve the imputation, and the psalmist on reflection owned he had spoken rashly, in a passion, and repented of it. Adam Clarke collects the renderings — in my light, in my excess or ecstasy, in my giddiness, in my fear or tremor, and in one old English version, when I was beside myself — and gives the sense as the moment when passion got the better of reason. On the charge he is harsher than Gill: the whole of man is a lie, falsity being diffused through his nature, so that he is imposed on by others and imposes in his turn, and no dependence can be placed on any until God converts the heart. He ends by asking who gives mankind this bad character, and answers, man.

The question of what to render is answered with a cup. Gill notes that the psalmist looks only to the Lord as the author of his mercies, saying nothing of his own merits or of the men who were instruments of good to him, at a loss how to make any return but determined to express a grateful sense of it. Charles Ellicott takes the cup as the drink offering that accompanied festival celebrations, and reports two rivals, the Passover cup, this psalm being sung as part of the festal group, and the figurative sense of cup as portion or lot. Gill rejects both the eucharistic reading and the cup of martyrdom, preferring an offering of praise, and compares the master of a family who takes up a cup at the close of a meal and gives thanks. Clarke describes that custom with its blessing of the Maker of the world who created the fruit of the vine, but prefers the libation offering, since the closing verses suggest a man standing in the temple.

Paying the vows is treated as a public act. C.H. Spurgeon calls it the third resolution and the start of its performance: good resolutions cannot be carried out too speedily, vows become debts and debts should be paid, and there is no more shame in having witnesses to a holy vow than to the payment of a just debt. He turns from there to the secret disciples and asks what they say to the verse. Gill makes the vows the resolutions taken in trouble, now made good before the assembled people as witnesses; Clarke supposes the offering was then being brought to the temple.

The verse on the death of the saints is read in two directions. Keil and Delitzsch infer that the saints are under God’s most especial providence, and apply to the word death the observation that what is precious we do not part with easily: their death is no trifling matter with him, he does not lightly suffer it to come about, and does not suffer his own to be torn away from him. Clarke reports the same construction, that the saints are too precious in the Lord’s sight to be lightly given over to death. Spurgeon takes the verse to explain why the psalmist was not allowed to die, and suggests the song was meant to remind families of mercies received when a member of the household had been sore sick and restored. Gill instead lets the saints die like other men, since Christ has abolished death as a punishment and taken away its curse and sting without taking away the thing itself, which remains for their good. Ellicott asks why the thought of death should intrude here, and answers that a recent deliverance is in view, the psalm reading naturally as thanksgiving for the survivors of some battle, whose grateful community would remember its dead.
16:
The closing profession is a claim of status, and each voice takes it differently. John Gill begins by distinguishing the grounds. A man is God’s servant by creation and under obligation for providential favours, but that is not what is meant here; the psalmist is a servant by the grace of God, which made him a willing one, and he is one in reality and not in name only, unlike those who say Lord, Lord and do not the will of God. The repetition Gill takes as deliberate, both a confirmation and a way of showing how heartily the man is attached to the service; and he is careful to add that nothing meritorious is being claimed. Standing in that character is an obligation to serve the Lord and no one else, and a ground on which protection may be expected, not a bill presented at the hand of God.

Adam Clarke hears the same words as the language of a household. Thou hast preserved me alive; I live with thee, for thee and to thee; I am thy willing domestic, the son of thine handmaid, like one born in thy house of a woman who was already thy property. Then he supplies the legal picture behind the phrase. A servant entitled to his freedom in the year of release might refuse to go out; and the man who refused had his ear bored to the door-post of his master’s house as evidence that he stayed by his own consent, to continue there for ever. That, Clarke says, is the position the psalmist claims: a servant made free by kindness who has chosen not to leave. Charles Ellicott draws a quieter inference from the same clause, that not the man only but his family stood within the covenant, and observes that the mother is named instead of the father, as is very commonly done in the East.

The sacrifice that follows is weighed against the older kind. Gill lists what it is offered for — deliverance from affliction and from death, the loosing of bonds in every sense, and all mercies temporal and spiritual alike — and holds that such sacrifices are according to the will of God, well pleasing to him when they are offered through Christ and in faith, and a glorifying of him. They are more acceptable, he adds, than all the ceremonial sacrifices, and it is for that reason that the psalmist determines to offer this one and not those. Clarke reads the same verses historically instead. If the psalm celebrates the deliverance from Babylon, as he thinks most probable, then it is no wonder to find the writer so intent on performing the rites of his religion in the temple at Jerusalem, a building that had been burnt with fire and was only then reviving out of its ruins, its service having been wholly interrupted for nearly four-score years.

The last verses fix the place. Gill treats the courts of the Lord’s house as an explanation of the earlier phrase about the presence of all his people: what was meant was the assembly of the saints gathered in the house of the Lord, at the door of the tabernacle and in the courts of it, where the people came together to worship. Clarke agrees that the writer speaks as one already present in the city, offering his vowed sacrifices in the temple. He closes by reporting how the psalm has been used rather than by pressing his own reading: most of it, he says, has been applied to Christ and his Church and taken in that way as prophetic, an accommodation he calls innocent and very edifying, and he notes that this is the interpretation the old Psalter gives of the whole.
